title: Cardiac Rhythm Response Simulation
description: Simulation on recognition of unstable dysrhythmias and early intervention priorities.

questions.prompt: A telemetry client becomes dizzy and hypotensive. Which rhythm changes are most concerning? Select all that apply.

choices.text: New-onset atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
Second-degree AV block with symptomatic bradycardia

questions.explanation: Sustained VT, rapid AF, and symptomatic second-degree AV block can each produce hemodynamic compromise (hypotension, dizziness, syncope). All three require urgent assessment and escalation. Normal sinus rhythm at 72/min does not contribute to the clinical deterioration described.
questions.rationale: Distinguishing hemodynamically stable from unstable dysrhythmias is a core NCLEX-RN content area. Rhythm recognition paired with clinical context (dizziness, hypotension) is the foundation of ACLS decision-making and safe telemetry nursing practice.

distractorRationale.C: Sinus rhythm at 72/min is a normal finding and is not a source of concern. Including this option tests whether learners can filter clinically irrelevant data from a complex presentation.

questions.prompt: Which action should the nurse take first for a pulseless ventricular tachycardia rhythm?

choices.text: Initiate CPR and activate the emergency response system.
Place the client in Trendelenburg position.

questions.explanation: Pulseless VT is a shockable cardiac arrest rhythm. The nurse must call for help and start CPR immediately. Early high-quality CPR and rapid defibrillation are the two interventions with the strongest evidence for survival. No assessment or medication step precedes CPR in a pulseless client.
questions.rationale: Cardiopulmonary arrest management follows the ACLS algorithm: confirm pulselessness, call for help, start CPR, deliver early defibrillation. Every minute of delay in defibrillation for pulseless VT/VF reduces survival to discharge by approximately 10%.

distractorRationale.B: A 12-lead ECG is contraindicated as the first action in a pulseless client. Confirmation of arrest is clinical (no pulse, unresponsive), not ECG-dependent. Delayed defibrillation worsens outcomes.
distractorRationale.C: Oral amiodarone has no role in pulseless arrest; IV/IO amiodarone is used in refractory pulseless VT/VF after initial shocks, not as a first action.
distractorRationale.D: Trendelenburg positioning is not recommended for cardiac arrest; CPR and defibrillation take absolute priority.
